strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored intersection (continual learning in cooperative MARL) and delivers the first dedicated CMARL benchmark with code, procedural generators, and solvability validation, enabling reproducible, essentially unbounded task sequences

Thoughtful engineering: end-to-end JAX/GPU acceleration enabling 100-task sequences on modest hardware, seed-controllable generation, and a documented layout validator (Appendix A) that guarantees playable kitchens

Well-designed evaluation protocol: normalized scoring with a programmatically computed layout-specific upper bound, standard CL metrics (Average Performance, Forgetting, Plasticity), multiple seeds with confidence intervals, and a plasticity-degradation analysis connecting to known single-agent pathologies
Informative ablations (multi-head outputs, task-ID conditioning, critic regularization, LayerNorm, CNN vs. MLP) that yield concrete, actionable findings for future CMARL work
Honest and thorough limitations section acknowledging narrow domain, full observability, two agents, and layout-only non-stationarity
weaknesses: Unsupported conclusion claims: the conclusion states that 'parameter-isolation methods fail to scale with longer task sequences,' yet no parameter-isolation method (e.g., PackNet) is evaluated anywhere in the experiments; similarly the claim of 'six continual learning methods' is inconsistent with the five methods actually benchmarked (one of which, FT, is a naive baseline, not a CL method)
The headline claim of '100 tasks' is not substantiated by any reported experiment: all main results (Figures 3-5) use 20-task sequences (10 for ablations, 10 repeated for plasticity)

Very narrow domain for a benchmark paper: only Overcooked, only two agents, only fully observable discrete-action settings, and all experiments use the dense (shaped) reward setting, despite the sparse setting being defined; results on the 25 handcrafted layouts promised in Section 4 are not reported
Baseline suite is dated and limited (EWC, Online EWC, MAS, L2, FT); no replay-based, architecture-based, or modern continual RL methods, limiting the benchmark's diagnostic value at release

Some evaluation concerns: the single-agent upper-bound normalization systematically underestimates the achievable optimum (acknowledged but makes cross-layout comparability approximate); Table 3 shows FPR > 1 for 3 repetitions which complicates the plasticity-loss narrative; ablations conducted only on Level 1

Writing has minor inconsistencies (e.g., 'Average Normalize Score' in Fig. 3 caption, task-incremental setting described with task ID 'accessible' during training but Fig. 5 ablates task-ID input) that should be clarified

strengths: Timely and underexplored problem: a benchmark for continual multi-agent RL fills a genuine gap, and the task-incremental formulation with standardized metrics (Average Performance, Forgetting, Plasticity) is clearly specified.

End-to-end JAX/GPU acceleration of both environment and training is an engineering contribution that meaningfully lowers the compute barrier for long task sequences (100 tasks in a few hours), and the procedural generator with a deterministic validator (Appendices A.2–A.3) is well documented and reproducible via seeds.
Honest and reasonably thorough limitations section, and adequate reproducibility: code is released, full hyperparameters, architecture details, and generator/validator pseudocode are provided.

The plasticity-loss experiment (Section 5.6, extending single-agent findings of Abbas et al. and Dohare et al. to a multi-agent setting) is a somewhat interesting empirical observation beyond the standard forgetting analysis.
weaknesses: Unsupported central claim: the abstract and Section 5.1 assert that CL+MARL combinations 'fail to scale to more complex settings requiring sustained coordination and adaptation,' but the main baseline comparison (Fig. 3, Table 2) and the ablation study (Fig. 5) are run only on Level 1 (6x6–7x7) layouts. Difficulty scaling is shown only for EWC (Fig. 7), so the headline negative claim is barely evidenced.

Internal inconsistency between results and conclusions: the conclusion claims 'parameter-isolation methods fail to scale with longer task sequences,' yet no parameter-isolation method (e.g., PackNet, cited in Related Work) appears in any experiment. Similarly, 'six continual learning methods' is claimed in the conclusion while five are evaluated.

Limited novelty: the benchmark is essentially JaxMARL's Overcooked plus procedural layout randomization and JAX wrappers of well-known CL methods. The 'first CMARL benchmark' claim is overstated given cited prior work on continual multi-agent coordination (e.g., Yuan et al. [35], which the paper itself cites); the distinction should be argued, not asserted.

Only one MARL algorithm (IPPO), two agents, fully observable state, discrete actions, and dense reward shaping in all main experiments; the sparse reward setting is defined but never evaluated. This substantially narrows what the benchmark conclusions actually cover.

The normalization scheme (dividing by a heuristic single-agent cook–deliver upper bound) is questionable: it is admitted to underestimate multi-agent throughput, so normalized scores are systematically biased differently across layouts, complicating cross-task and cross-method comparisons; scores above 1 further complicate interpretation.

Results are largely predictable (FT forgets, EWC/L2 retain but sacrifice plasticity) and the multi-head ablation outcome is nearly tautological given the task-incremental setup with per-task output heads. The contribution is a testbed, but the scientific insight generated so far is thin.

Experimental rigor gaps: no significance testing despite small differences (e.g., EWC 0.839±0.03 vs. Online EWC 0.769±0.09), 5 seeds only, inconsistent sequence lengths between baseline (20 tasks) and ablation (10 tasks) experiments, and single-run plasticity tables (Table 3) without variance.

Presentation sloppiness undermines confidence: 'Average Normalize Score' (Figs. 3, 7), error bars described as 95% CIs in Figure 4/5 but ±1 s.e. in Figure 6, and a confusing Table 1 (e.g., CORA marked GPU-accelerated; 'No. Tasks ∞' for MEAL).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated gap: continual learning in cooperative multi-agent RL is underexplored, and the paper positions MEAL as the first benchmark for this intersection, with a useful comparison table against existing CL and MARL benchmarks (Table 1).

The JAX-based, end-to-end GPU-accelerated pipeline is a genuine practical contribution: it makes long task sequences (up to 100 tasks) feasible on modest hardware, addressing a real computational bottleneck of prior CL benchmarks.

Procedural environment generation is carefully engineered and documented: the generator pipeline, solvability validator (R1–R10), and single-agent upper-bound normalization (Appendix A.1–A.3) are specified in enough detail (with code listings and hyperparameters) to be reproducible, and seeds control task generation for fair comparison.

The evaluation is methodologically sensible: standard Average Performance / Forgetting / Plasticity metrics, 5 seeds with 95% confidence intervals, per-task forgetting visualizations (Fig. 4), and a plasticity-degradation experiment following established metrics (AUC-loss, FPR, RAUC).

The ablation study (Fig. 5) yields actionable findings, e.g., multi-head outputs are critical, task-ID input is negligible, and layer norm interacts with method-specific mechanisms (L2 scale drift), and the limitations section is honest about the narrow domain, two-agent/fully-observable restriction, and layout-only task shifts.
weaknesses: Experimental coverage is narrower than the headline claims. The abstract and Table 1 emphasize 100-task sequences, but the main experiments use 20-task Level 1 sequences; the difficulty-level comparison (Fig. 7) only shows EWC, and hard levels remain essentially unexplored by all but one method.

The domain is a single environment family (Overcooked). Generalization of the benchmark's conclusions beyond grid-based cooperative kitchens is untested, and the paper's own limitations concede this; more diverse multi-agent tasks would strengthen the claim of a general CMARL benchmark.

Multi-agent-specific analysis is thin. The introduction argues that CMARL poses unique challenges (convention breakdown, inter-agent forgetting), but the results and analyses largely mirror known single-agent CL findings (regularization retains, FT forgets, plasticity loss). There is no behavioral analysis of coordination/roles, and no comparison with the existing multi-agent continual coordination work the paper itself cites [34, 35].

Some inconsistencies and unsupported statements: the conclusion mentions 'six continual learning methods' while five are evaluated and described; the conclusion claims 'parameter-isolation methods fail to scale with longer task sequences', yet no parameter-isolation method (e.g., PackNet, discussed in related work) is actually evaluated.

The score normalization uses a single-agent optimal cycle as the denominator. Since two agents can exceed this bound, normalized scores are unbounded above (e.g., FT plasticity P = 1.163 > 1), which complicates interpretation of the metrics and cross-task comparability the normalization is meant to provide.

The plasticity analysis is noisy and only partially convincing: degradation is stated to occur 'in most tasks' with some tasks (8, 9) unchanged, and RAUC falls only 6.5%; the evidence for plasticity loss on MEAL is suggestive rather than decisive.

Baseline set is limited to regularization-based methods plus fine-tuning; replay-based and architectural methods central to the CL literature are absent, so the finding that 'naïve combinations fail' is not tested against the strongest CL families.

strengths: Fills a genuine gap: there is currently no dedicated benchmark for continual multi-agent RL, and the paper makes a convincing case that existing CRL benchmarks (Continual World, COOM, CORA) and MARL suites (SMAC, MPE, Melting Pot) are ill-suited for this intersection (Table 1).

The procedural layout generator with a deterministic solvability validator (Appendices A.1–A.3) is a thoughtful design: it provides a virtually unbounded, seed-controlled supply of verified solvable tasks, with well-documented complexity analysis and failure handling.
The end-to-end JAX pipeline enabling 100-task sequences on a single desktop GPU is a meaningful systems contribution, and the throughput claims (5 min/task) are concrete and plausibly reproducible.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for a benchmark paper: six CL baselines across three difficulty levels with confidence intervals (Tables 2, 10–12), ablations of five architectural components (Fig. 6), N-agent scaling (Table 3), plasticity-loss analysis (Sec. 5.5, App. G), reward design (Table 5), partial observability (Sec. 5.7), curriculum learning (App. E), and designated roles (App. H).

The paper extracts real insights beyond just releasing a testbed: the stability–plasticity trade-off (Fig. 4), the EWC vs. Online EWC rigidity analysis on Level 3 (App. C), the finding that multi-head architectures dominate all other factors (Fig. 6), and the observation that MAPPO's centralized critic transfers poorly in CL regimes (Sec. 5.7).

Reproducibility is strong: complete hyperparameter tables (Table 6), network details, seeds, evaluation protocol, and public code. The limitations section is honest about discrete actions, the narrow Overcooked domain, and the task-incremental restriction.
weaknesses: The task-incremental setup with known task IDs and per-task multi-head outputs substantially weakens the 'continual learning' challenge. The paper's own ablation shows removing multi-heads devastates performance across all methods (Fig. 6), which suggests most of the reported performance comes from task-specific head selection rather than learning to retain and transfer coordination. With layout-only variation between tasks, shared dynamics, and oracle task identity at evaluation, the benchmark risks measuring per-task specialization plus backbone transfer rather than genuine continual learning; the paper would benefit from framing or additional non-task-incremental (task-agnostic) experiments.

Level 3 is largely unsolved by all baselines (best average score 0.306), making that difficulty level poorly discriminative between methods in its current form; conversely, on Level 1, standard EWC with a multi-head IPPO already achieves 0.839, leaving a very wide unsolved band in between. The difficulty calibration could be discussed more carefully.

Several analytical explanations are speculative and presented without supporting experiments, e.g., the account of why MAPPO underperforms IPPO under PO (cross-task critic drift), the layer-norm/L2 interaction, and the plasticity-loss attenuation hypothesis attributed to multi-heads.

The benchmark's generality is narrow: a single environment family (Overcooked), two-agent default, discrete actions, and layout-only task shifts. The claimed importance of CMARL (partner non-stationarity, role forgetting, convention breakdown) is only partially exercised, since partner policies and dynamics never change across tasks.

Some claims are asserted rather than demonstrated, such as 'first end-to-end GPU-accelerated continual RL library' and the characterization of existing benchmarks in Table 1 (e.g., marking Google Football as GPU-accelerated is debatable); these should be softened or verified.

Forgetting and forward transfer metrics inherit design choices (last-k-step averages, AUC against a single-task baseline) whose sensitivity is not analyzed; e.g., how results change with k, or with the simplifying single-agent optimality bound used for normalization (which understates multi-agent upper bounds, as the authors themselves note in App. A.1).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: continual learning in cooperative MARL is underexplored, and no existing benchmark combines multi-agent coordination with continual evaluation (Table 1 comparison is convincing).

The JAX-based end-to-end pipeline is a practical contribution: ~5 minutes per 1e7-step task on a single A100 enables 100-task sequences, which prior CPU-bound CRL benchmarks cannot support. The infrastructure claims are backed by concrete runtime numbers.

The experimental scope is extensive for a benchmark paper: six CL methods across three difficulty levels, ablations (multi-head, task ID, critic reg, layer norm, CNN), N-agent scaling (Table 3), plasticity analysis (Section 5.5), reward design (Table 5), partial observability (Section 5.7), and curriculum (Appendix E), with confidence intervals in Appendix J.

The environment engineering is careful: a deterministic layout validator with ten explicit checks (Appendix A.3), seed-controlled generation for reproducibility, and a per-layout normalized score computed from a single-agent optimal cook-deliver cycle (Appendix A.1).

Limitations are discussed honestly (Section 7): discrete actions only, narrow domain, task-incremental-only evaluation, and no dynamics/partner drift. Hyperparameters, architecture details, and code release support reproducibility.

Several findings are genuinely informative, e.g., the EWC-vs-Online-EWC analysis (Appendix C) explaining why cumulative Fisher penalties fail on Level 3, and the counterintuitive result that MAPPO underperforms IPPO in the CL regime (Section 5.7).
weaknesses: The benchmark design substantially weakens its own central purpose. The default setting is task-incremental with multi-head outputs and one-hot task IDs, which effectively gives each task its own output slice. The paper itself reports 'near-perfect retention' for EWC on Level 1 (Figure 3 middle) and near-zero forgetting, meaning catastrophic forgetting — the phenomenon CMARL is supposed to expose — barely manifests for well-configured methods. Conclusions about CL method failures therefore conflate architectural choices with continual-learning difficulty, and it is unclear the benchmark measures what it claims to measure.

The domain is very narrow for a 'benchmark': a single environment (Overcooked) with layout variation only. All claims about CMARL dynamics rest on one grid-world game; no evidence is offered that findings (e.g., EWC dominance, multi-head necessity) transfer to other cooperative domains. This limits the generality of the takeaways more than the limitations section acknowledges.

The normalization upper bound assumes a single optimal agent, so scores above 1 indicate cooperation, but the floor for uncoordinated/random behavior is unbounded and layout-dependent; the paper does not report the distribution of achievable scores per layout, making metric interpretation across heterogeneous layouts harder than presented.

Some headline claims are stretched relative to evidence: the conclusion states 'a simple curriculum boosts performance on complex layouts,' but Appendix E shows no statistically significant difference on Level 2 and a single comparison on Level 3 with overlapping variance (0.653±0.181 vs 0.328±0.238, n=5 seeds). Similarly, the plasticity-loss hypothesis attributing mild degradation to multi-heads is acknowledged as speculation but presented alongside conclusions.

The evaluated CL method set is dated and mostly regularization-based (EWC, Online EWC, L2, MAS, AGEM, FT). Notably absent are architectural methods cited in the related work (PackNet) and modern CRL approaches [9, 10, 17], so the claim that 'naïvely combining popular CL and MARL methods fails' is tested against a limited slice of the design space.

The 'first' claims (first CMARL benchmark, first GPU-accelerated continual RL library) are asserted rather than defended; given related systems like JaxMARL and open-environment MARL work [44, 45], a more careful delineation would be appropriate.

Difficulty is defined primarily by grid size and obstacle density; the paper provides only qualitative justification that Level 3 'requires deliberate cooperation' (Figure 2), with no quantitative measurement of coordination demands, so the mapping from difficulty level to the CMARL-specific challenges of interest is under-evidenced.

strengths: Genuine gap addressed: MEAL is plausibly the first benchmark purpose-built for continual multi-agent RL, and the JAX-based, GPU-accelerated task-sequence pipeline (100 tasks on a single desktop GPU) is a concrete and valuable systems contribution that removes a real bottleneck in existing CPU-bound CL benchmarks.

The environment engineering is careful and well-documented: procedural generation with solvability validation (Appendices A.1–A.3), difficulty levels defined by observable layout parameters, a principled per-layout normalization bound, and seeded reproducibility. The appendices contain enough detail (hyperparameters, architecture, validator logic, code listings) to support reproduction.

Evaluation is broad and mostly well-designed: six CL methods across three difficulty levels with 5 seeds and 95% CIs, an informative ablation (multi-head outputs emerge as the decisive component), and five additional studies (N-agent scaling, plasticity loss under repetition, reward design, partial observability, curriculum, designated roles) that go well beyond a minimal benchmark release.

The paper is honest about its limitations (discrete actions only, narrow Overcooked domain, task-incremental-only setting, no dynamics/partner shifts), and several results (e.g., MAPPO underperforming IPPO under PO; curriculum gains on hard layouts) are reported as observations with clearly flagged plausible explanations rather than overclaimed.
Qualitative analysis (failure modes in Figure 13, per-task forgetting/transfer curves in Figures 16–17) adds genuine insight into why methods fail in this setting.
weaknesses: The adopted task-incremental setting with known task identity and multi-head (per-task-slice) outputs substantially weakens the benchmark's realism and the significance of its headline conclusions. The ablation showing that multi-head architectures are 'most critical' effectively means the benchmark primarily measures retention in a shared trunk when task IDs are given and output interference is architecturally removed — a much easier problem than the domain-general continual MARL the introduction motivates (e.g., autonomous vehicles adapting to unseen conditions without task labels). Methods are never evaluated in the harder task-free setting.

Domain narrowness: all tasks are procedurally generated Overcooked layouts, so 'continual learning' here amounts to layout changes with identical dynamics, rewards, and action semantics. The claimed generality of CMARL conclusions rests on a single environment family; at least one additional environment type would be needed to support the framing that MEAL is a general CMARL benchmark rather than an Overcooked-CMARL benchmark.

The normalization scheme (single-agent optimal cycle) means scores above 1 reflect cooperation, but the upper bound deliberately ignores multi-agent parallelism; the paper acknowledges this, yet the implications for cross-layout comparability of A/F/FT (e.g., whether forgetting on parallelizable layouts is systematically over- or under-counted) are not analyzed.

Some central claims rest on thin evidence: EWC's Level 2 average score has very wide variance (0.604±0.21, Table 11), making the EWC-vs-Online-EWC comparisons at that level fragile; the MAPPO-underperformance explanation in Section 5.7 is explicitly speculative; and several mechanistic explanations (plasticity differences due to multi-heads, curriculum effects) are hypotheses rather than tested.

Baseline coverage is conservative: all six CL methods are regularization/architecture/replay variants from the 2017–2018 supervised CL literature; more recent continual RL methods (e.g., those cited in the related work on scalability, memory efficiency, and stability [9, 10, 17]) are not evaluated, limiting the benchmark's usefulness as a current state-of-the-art reference point.

Reproducibility of results depends on a GitHub repository whose contents cannot be verified from the manuscript; no proof-of-quality signals (tests, license, or external reproduction) are provided in the paper itself.
